\section{Introduction}

Emmy Noether's ascending chain condition (ACC)---every ascending chain of ideals
eventually stabilizes---is the dividing line between the tame and the wild in
commutative algebra. Noetherian rings support the finiteness theorems on which
algebraic geometry and number theory rest; non-Noetherian rings are their unruly
complement. This paper adopts a deliberately geometric view of that complement.

An \emph{Escher staircase} is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals. The name
recalls M.~C.~Escher's \emph{Ascending and Descending}, in which a staircase rises
through four flights only to return to its origin. Our flagship staircases have exactly
this property at the level of the ideal lattice: they climb strictly forever, yet the
meet of all their rungs is the zero ideal, the bottom rung from which the ascent
starts. The failure of ACC is thus literalized as an impossible architecture.

Our contributions are: (1) a characterization that a commutative ring admits an Escher
staircase iff it is not Noetherian (Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant}); (2) two explicit,
verified staircases with the loop-back property (Theorems~\ref{thm:pi} and
\ref{thm:var}), together with a sharp finite/infinite dichotomy for polynomial rings
(Theorem~\ref{thm:dichotomy}); (3) a negative instance, the $p$-adic integers
(Theorem~\ref{thm:padic}); and (4) three transfer laws for products
(Theorem~\ref{thm:prod}), single-variable adjunction (Theorem~\ref{thm:poly}), and
subring inclusion (Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}). The last is the ``collapse''
phenomenon and shows the invariant is emphatically not monotone under subrings.

\section{Definitions and preliminaries}

Throughout, $R$ and $S$ denote commutative rings with unit. An \emph{ideal} of $R$ is
an additive subgroup $I \subseteq R$ with $rI \subseteq I$ for all $r \in R$. The
ideals of $R$ form a complete lattice $(\Ideal(R), \subseteq)$ with bottom
$\bot = \{0\}$, top $R$, meets given by intersection, and joins by ideal sum. For a
family $\{I_n\}$ the meet is $\bigwedge_n I_n = \bigcap_n I_n$.

\begin{definition}[Escher staircase]
An \emph{Escher staircase} in $R$ is a strictly monotone map
$I : \NN \to \Ideal(R)$; equivalently, an infinite chain
$I_0 \subsetneq I_1 \subsetneq I_2 \subsetneq \cdots$ of ideals. We write $\Esc(R)$ for
the proposition ``$R$ admits an Escher staircase.''
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Noetherian ring]
$R$ is \emph{Noetherian} if every ascending chain of ideals is eventually constant;
equivalently, there is no strictly increasing $\NN$-indexed chain of ideals.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[loop-back]
An Escher staircase $\{I_n\}$ \emph{loops back} if $\bigwedge_n I_n = I_0$. Since the
chain is ascending this always holds; the terminology is reserved for the striking case
$I_0 = \bot$, where the infimum of an infinite strict ascent is the zero ideal.
\end{definition}

We use two facts repeatedly. \emph{Surjective inheritance}: if $\varphi : A \to B$ is a
surjective ring homomorphism and $A$ is Noetherian, then $B$ is Noetherian. The
\emph{Hilbert Basis Theorem}: if $R$ is Noetherian, so is $R[x]$.

\section{The invariant theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Escher staircase $=$ non-Noetherian]\label{thm:invariant}
For every commutative ring $R$,
\[ \Esc(R) \iff R \text{ is not Noetherian.} \]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Being Noetherian is, by definition, the nonexistence of a strictly increasing
$\NN$-chain of ideals. An Escher staircase is by definition exactly such a chain. Thus
$R$ is non-Noetherian iff a strictly increasing chain exists. In one direction a
strictly monotone chain witnesses non-well-foundedness directly; in the other,
non-well-foundedness of an $\NN$-indexed order yields an order embedding of
$(\NN, <)$, whose image is a strictly increasing chain.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant} is the load-bearing bridge: every transfer law below is
proved by transporting the corresponding Noetherian transfer law across this
equivalence.

\section{Explicit staircases and the negative instance}

\subsection{The tail-vanishing staircase in $\prod_{\NN}\ZZ$}

Let $R = \prod_{n\in\NN}\ZZ$ be the ring of integer sequences under coordinatewise
operations. For $n \in \NN$ define $S_n = \{ f \in R : f_k = 0 \text{ for all } k \ge n\}$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:Sn}
Each $S_n$ is an ideal, and $n \mapsto S_n$ is monotone.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Closure under addition and multiplication by arbitrary sequences is coordinatewise;
monotonicity holds because $m \le n$ and $f_k = 0$ for $k \ge m$ force $f_k = 0$ for
$k \ge n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[explicit staircase in $\prod_\NN\ZZ$]\label{thm:pi}
The chain $S_0 \subsetneq S_1 \subsetneq \cdots$ is an Escher staircase with
$S_0 = \bot$ and $\bigwedge_n S_n = \bot$; it loops back.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $e_n$ be the indicator sequence with a $1$ in position $n$. Then
$e_n \in S_{n+1}\setminus S_n$, so $S_n \subsetneq S_{n+1}$ and the chain is strictly
monotone. Membership $f \in S_0$ forces $f = 0$, so $S_0 = \bot$; hence
$\bigwedge_n S_n \subseteq S_0 = \bot$, giving loop-back.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\prod_\NN\ZZ$ is not Noetherian.
\end{corollary}

\subsection{The variable staircase in $k[x_0, x_1, \dots]$}

Let $k$ be a field, $R = k[x_0, x_1, \dots]$, and $V_n = \langle x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}\rangle$.

\begin{lemma}[missing-variable non-membership]\label{lem:missing}
For a finite $s \subseteq \NN$ and $j \notin s$, $x_j \notin \langle \{x_i : i \in s\}\rangle$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The $k$-algebra endomorphism $\varphi_s$ sending $x_i \mapsto 0$ for $i \in s$ and
fixing the rest annihilates $\langle\{x_i : i\in s\}\rangle$. If $x_j$ lay in it we
would get $x_j = \varphi_s(x_j) = 0$, contradicting $x_j \ne 0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[variable staircase]\label{thm:var}
$V_0 \subsetneq V_1 \subsetneq \cdots$ is an Escher staircase with $V_0 = \bot$ and
$\bigwedge_n V_n = \bot$; it loops back.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Lemma~\ref{lem:missing} with $s = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$, $j = n$ gives
$x_n \in V_{n+1}\setminus V_n$, so the chain is strictly monotone; $V_0 = \bot$ gives
loop-back.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Dichotomy and negative instance}

\begin{theorem}[polynomial dichotomy]\label{thm:dichotomy}
Over a field $k$: for every finite $n$, $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ admits no Escher
staircase, while $k[x_0, x_1, \dots]$ does. In particular $k[x]$ admits no staircase.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
By the Hilbert Basis Theorem and induction, $k[x_1, \dots, x_n]$ is Noetherian, so by
Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant} it admits no staircase; the positive half is
Theorem~\ref{thm:var}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[no staircase in the $p$-adics]\label{thm:padic}
For each prime $p$, the ring $\ZZ_p$ of $p$-adic integers admits no Escher staircase.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$\ZZ_p$ is a discrete valuation ring, hence a principal ideal domain, hence
Noetherian; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant}.
\end{proof}

\section{Transfer laws}

\subsection{Finite products: a local-to-global obstruction}

\begin{theorem}[product law]\label{thm:prod}
$\Esc(R \times S) \iff \Esc(R) \lor \Esc(S)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
It suffices to show $R \times S$ is Noetherian iff both factors are. The projections
$\pi_R, \pi_S$ are surjective, so a Noetherian product forces Noetherian factors;
conversely a finite product of Noetherian rings is Noetherian. Negate and apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant}.
\end{proof}

The staircase of a finite product is always witnessed inside a single coordinate.

\begin{example}
With $R = \QQ[x_0, x_1, \dots]$ (a staircase) and $S = \QQ$ (none), $R \times S$ admits
a staircase, lifted from the first coordinate.
\end{example}

\subsection{Single-variable adjunction is neutral}

\begin{theorem}[single variable is neutral]\label{thm:poly}
$\Esc(R[x]) \iff \Esc(R)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The evaluation $\mathrm{ev}_0 : R[x] \to R$, $x \mapsto 0$, is surjective (right
inverse $C$), so $R[x]$ Noetherian implies $R$ Noetherian; conversely the Hilbert Basis
Theorem gives the reverse. Negate and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorems~\ref{thm:dichotomy} and \ref{thm:poly} together show that no single variable
creates or destroys the staircase; only the passage from finitely to infinitely many
variables can.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The collapse: non-monotonicity under subrings}

\begin{theorem}[subring collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
There is an injective ring homomorphism $\iota : A \hookrightarrow B$ with $\Esc(A)$
true and $\Esc(B)$ false. Concretely $A = \QQ[x_0, x_1, \dots]$ and
$B = \Frac(A) = \QQ(x_0, x_1, \dots)$, with $\iota$ the canonical inclusion.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
$A$ is an integral domain, so the map into $\Frac(A)$ is injective; $\Esc(A)$ holds by
Theorem~\ref{thm:var}. But $B$ is a field, whose only ideals are $\bot$ and $B$, so it
is Noetherian and $\Esc(B)$ fails by Theorem~\ref{thm:invariant}.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
$\Esc(-)$ is not preserved by injective ring homomorphisms: a subring can be strictly
further from Noetherian than a ring containing it.
\end{corollary}

Downstairs the tower $\langle x_0\rangle \subsetneq \langle x_0, x_1\rangle \subsetneq
\cdots$ climbs forever; upstairs every nonzero element is invertible, so each rung
generates the unit ideal and the tower collapses. This is the crispest algebraic form
of Escher's illusion.

\section{Discussion and future directions}

The Escher staircase repackages ACC as a concrete, climbable object and exposes an
asymmetry easy to overlook abstractly: the invariant transports covariantly along
surjections but is broken along inclusions. A ring may be more tangled than every ring
containing it, and that excess is a genuine, exhibitable staircase.

Three programs suggest themselves. First, a numerical \emph{Escher height}: the longest
chain of prime ideals threadable strictly between consecutive rungs of a grounded
ascending chain, conjecturally zero for finitely many variables, infinite for countably
many, and equal to the Krull dimension ($=2$) for integer-valued polynomials. Second,
the ring of all algebraic integers, conjecturally carrying a staircase of dyadic
radicals of $2$ with height exactly one. Third, a precise description of which
localizations of $k[x_0, x_1, \dots]$ preserve or destroy the variable staircase:
inverting finitely many elements preserves it, inverting infinitely many destroys it.

\section{Conclusion}

An Escher staircase---an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals that loops back to
its zero-ideal floor---is a faithful, pictorial name for the failure of the ascending
chain condition. It exists exactly in the non-Noetherian rings; it can be built by hand
in the countable integer product and in polynomial rings with infinitely many
variables; and it is forbidden in Noetherian rings such as the $p$-adics and
finite-variable polynomial rings. Its transfer laws are covariant along surjections but
broken along inclusions: a subring can carry a staircase that collapses the instant one
steps up to an overring.

    I_0  <  I_1  <  I_2  <  ...

that "loops back": the meet (intersection) of the whole ascending tower equals the

This script demonstrates, with fully explicit finite windows:

  1. The tail-vanishing staircase  S_n = {f : f_k = 0 for all k >= n}  in the
     product ring of integer sequences, with the indicator witness separating each
     step and the loop-back to {0}.

  2. The variable staircase  V_n = <x_0, ..., x_{n-1}>  in the polynomial ring in
     countably many variables, with monomial-ideal membership tested by divisibility.

  3. The product transfer law: R x S has a staircase iff a factor does.

  4. The collapse: each rung V_n is a proper ideal of the polynomial ring, but
     generates the WHOLE fraction field once nonzero elements become invertible.

Everything is self-contained; no third-party libraries are required.

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The tail-vanishing staircase  S_n  in the product ring of integer sequences
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# We model a "finitely supported" integer sequence as a dict {index: value} with
# only nonzero entries stored.  A sequence f belongs to S_n iff every stored index
# is < n (i.e. f_k = 0 for all k >= n).

Sequence_ = Dict[int, int]


def in_tail_zero_ideal(f: Sequence_, n: int) -> bool:
    """Return True iff f in S_n, i.e. f_k = 0 for all k >= n."""
    return all(index < n for index, value in f.items() if value != 0)


def indicator(n: int) -> Sequence_:
    """The indicator sequence e_n: value 1 at position n, 0 elsewhere."""
    return {n: 1}


def demo_tail_staircase(depth: int = 6) -> None:
    """Certify that S_0 < S_1 < ... is a strictly ascending, looping staircase."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. Tail-vanishing staircase  S_n  in the ring of integer sequences")
    print("=" * 70)
    for n in range(depth):
        e = indicator(n)  # witness for the strict jump S_n < S_{n+1}
        in_next = in_tail_zero_ideal(e, n + 1)
        in_here = in_tail_zero_ideal(e, n)
        strict = in_next and not in_here
        print(
            f"  e_{n} = (1 at pos {n})  in S_{n+1}: {in_next},  in S_{n}: {in_here}"
            f"   =>  S_{n} < S_{n+1}: {strict}"
        )
    # loop-back: only the zero sequence lies in S_0, hence in the whole meet.
    only_zero_in_S0 = in_tail_zero_ideal({}, 0) and not in_tail_zero_ideal({0: 1}, 0)
    print(f"  S_0 = {{0}} (only the zero sequence): {only_zero_in_S0}")
    print("  => meet of all S_n = S_0 = {0}: the staircase loops back.\n")

# 2. The variable staircase  V_n = <x_0, ..., x_{n-1}>  (monomial ideals)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# A monomial in x_0, x_1, ... is an exponent vector, stored as a tuple of
# (variable_index, exponent) pairs with positive exponents, sorted by index.
# A monomial m lies in the monomial ideal generated by variables in a set S iff
# some variable x_i with i in S divides m, i.e. m has positive exponent at i.

Monomial = Tuple[Tuple[int, int], ...]


def monomial(**powers: int) -> Monomial:
    """Build a monomial from keyword powers, e.g. monomial(x0=2, x1=1)."""
    items = []
    for name, exp in powers.items():
        if exp > 0:
            items.append((int(name[1:]), exp))
    return tuple(sorted(items))


def variable(i: int) -> Monomial:
    """The bare variable x_i as a monomial."""
    return ((i, 1),)


def in_variable_ideal(m: Monomial, gens: Set[int]) -> bool:
    """Return True iff monomial m lies in the ideal generated by {x_i : i in gens}."""
    return any(exp > 0 and idx in gens for idx, exp in m)

    print("2. Variable staircase  V_n = <x_0, ..., x_{n-1}>  in k[x_0, x_1, ...]")
    print("=" * 70)
    for n in range(depth):
        gens_next: Set[int] = set(range(n + 1))  # V_{n+1} = <x_0,...,x_n>
        gens_here: Set[int] = set(range(n))      # V_n     = <x_0,...,x_{n-1}>

An *Escher staircase* in a commutative ring is an infinite strictly ascending chain
of ideals

that "loops back": the meet (intersection) of the whole ascending tower equals the

commutative ring admits such a staircase if and only if it is NOT Noetherian.

  2. The variable staircase  V_n = <x_0, ..., x_{n-1}>  in the polynomial ring in

  3. The product transfer law: R x S has a staircase iff a factor does.

  4. The collapse: each rung V_n is a proper ideal of the polynomial ring, but

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The tail-vanishing staircase  S_n  in the product ring of integer sequences
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# We model a "finitely supported" integer sequence as a dict {index: value} with
# only nonzero entries stored.  A sequence f belongs to S_n iff every stored index
# is < n (i.e. f_k = 0 for all k >= n).

Sequence_ = Dict[int, int]


def in_tail_zero_ideal(f: Sequence_, n: int) -> bool:
    """Return True iff f in S_n, i.e. f_k = 0 for all k >= n."""
    return all(index < n for index, value in f.items() if value != 0)


def indicator(n: int) -> Sequence_:
    """The indicator sequence e_n: value 1 at position n, 0 elsewhere."""
    return {n: 1}


def demo_tail_staircase(depth: int = 6) -> None:
    """Certify that S_0 < S_1 < ... is a strictly ascending, looping staircase."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("1. Tail-vanishing staircase  S_n  in the ring of integer sequences")
    print("=" * 70)
    for n in range(depth):
        e = indicator(n)  # witness for the strict jump S_n < S_{n+1}
        in_next = in_tail_zero_ideal(e, n + 1)
        in_here = in_tail_zero_ideal(e, n)
        strict = in_next and not in_here
        print(
            f"  e_{n} = (1 at pos {n})  in S_{n+1}: {in_next},  in S_{n}: {in_here}"
            f"   =>  S_{n} < S_{n+1}: {strict}"
        )
    # loop-back: only the zero sequence lies in S_0, hence in the whole meet.
    only_zero_in_S0 = in_tail_zero_ideal({}, 0) and not in_tail_zero_ideal({0: 1}, 0)
    print(f"  S_0 = {{0}} (only the zero sequence): {only_zero_in_S0}")
    print("  => meet of all S_n = S_0 = {0}: the staircase loops back.\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. The variable staircase  V_n = <x_0, ..., x_{n-1}>  (monomial ideals)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

# A monomial in x_0, x_1, ... is an exponent vector, stored as a tuple of
# (variable_index, exponent) pairs with positive exponents, sorted by index.
# A monomial m lies in the monomial ideal generated by variables in a set S iff
# some variable x_i with i in S divides m, i.e. m has positive exponent at i.

Monomial = Tuple[Tuple[int, int], ...]


def monomial(**powers: int) -> Monomial:
    """Build a monomial from keyword powers, e.g. monomial(x0=2, x1=1)."""
    items = []
    for name, exp in powers.items():
        if exp > 0:
            items.append((int(name[1:]), exp))
    return tuple(sorted(items))


def variable(i: int) -> Monomial:
    """The bare variable x_i as a monomial."""
    return ((i, 1),)


def in_variable_ideal(m: Monomial, gens: Set[int]) -> bool:
    """Return True iff monomial m lies in the ideal generated by {x_i : i in gens}."""
    return any(exp > 0 and idx in gens for idx, exp in m)


def demo_variable_staircase(depth: int = 6) -> None:
    """Certify x_n in V_{n+1} \\ V_n, so V_0 < V_1 < ... is strictly ascending."""
    print("=" * 70)
    print("2. Variable staircase  V_n = <x_0, ..., x_{n-1}>  in k[x_0, x_1, ...]")

            f"   =>  V_{n} < V_{n+1}: {in_next and not in_here}"

    print("  V_0 = <empty> = {0}; meet of all V_n = V_0 = {0}: loops back.\n")

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def escher_product(has_staircase_R: bool, has_staircase_S: bool) -> bool:
    """The transfer law: a finite product has a staircase iff some factor does."""
    return has_staircase_R or has_staircase_S


def demo_product_law() -> None:
    print("=" * 70)
    print("3. Product transfer law:  Esc(R x S)  <=>  Esc(R) or Esc(S)")
    print("=" * 70)
    cases: List[Tuple[str, bool, str, bool]] = [
        ("Q[x_0,x_1,...]", True, "Q", False),   # staircase x none
        ("Q", False, "Q", False),               # none x none
        ("Q[x_0,x_1,...]", True, "Z^N", True),  # staircase x staircase
        ("Z_p", False, "Q[x_0,x_1,...]", True), # none x staircase
    ]
    for nameR, escR, nameS, escS in cases:
        result = escher_product(escR, escS)
        witness = (
            "left coordinate" if escR else "right coordinate" if escS else "none"
        )
        print(
            f"  ({nameR}) x ({nameS}):  Esc = {result}"
            f"   (witnessing coordinate: {witness})"
        )
    print()

# 4. The collapse:  V_n proper in the ring, but = (1) in the fraction field
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def rung_generates_unit_in_field(gens: Set[int]) -> bool:
    """In a field every nonzero ideal is the whole ring: a nonempty rung swells to (1)."""
    return len(gens) > 0

    print("=" * 70)

    print("=" * 70)

        )

    demo_product_law()
    demo_collapse()
    print("All demonstrations completed.")
